title: NYTimes Analysis
text:
Dataset: NYTimes Article Headlines
This analysis uses the NYTimes dataset from the RTextTools package. The dataset contains article IDs, publication dates, article headlines, article subjects, and topic codes for articles from the New York Times from 1996 to 2006. The dataset was compiled by Professor Amber E. Boydstun at the University of California, Davis.
The following graph shows the number of articles published each month from 1996-2006. Upon first inspection, February has the least number of articles published, and January, March, May, and December seem to have the most number of articles published. If we stop to consider why this might be, we quickly notice that February has the fewest days and January, March, May, and December all have 31 days. We inspect this further in the following graph.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(RTextTools)
data(NYTimes)
head(as_tibble(NYTimes), 4)


# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Article_ID Date     Title                                   Subject Topic.Code
       <int> <fct>    <fct>                                   <fct>        <int>
1      41246 1-Jan-96 Nation's Smaller Jails Struggle To Cop… Jails …         12
2      41257 2-Jan-96 FEDERAL IMPASSE SADDLING STATES WITH I… Federa…         20
3      41268 3-Jan-96 Long, Costly Prelude Does Little To Al… Conten…         20
4      41279 4-Jan-96 Top Leader of the Bosnian Serbs Now Un… Bosnia…         19


Code
#Adding a column onlyMonth that has extracts the "Jan" or similar from the date column using regular expressions. Converting this column into factors allows us to order the months chronologically. I grouped by this column and then plotted the number of articles published each month to get the following graph:
grouped_month <- NYTimes |> mutate(onlyMonth = factor(str_extract(Date, "(?<=-)[a-z|A-Z]+"), levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"))) |> group_by(onlyMonth)
#NYTimes <- fct_relevel(onlyMonth, levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"))
ggplot(grouped_month, aes(x = onlyMonth)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "", subtitle = "Number of Articles Published", title = "Number of Articles Published Each Month from 1996-2006")









The graph below more clearly shows that more articles are published during months with more days. Although we can’t prove why this is, the New York Times is published every day, meaning that months with more days likely have a higher quantity of articles simply because they have more editions published.


Code
#Groups the months based on the number of days in each month, and then computes the average number of articles published in each month in the period from 1996-2006.
new_grouped_month <- grouped_month |> mutate(numDays = ifelse(str_detect(onlyMonth, "Feb"), "28/29", ifelse(str_detect(onlyMonth, "Jan|Mar|May|Jul|Aug|Oct|Dec"), "31", "30"))) |> group_by(numDays) |> summarize(count = n()) |> mutate(average = ifelse(numDays == "31", count/7, ifelse(numDays == "30", count/4, count)))

ggplot(new_grouped_month, aes(x = numDays, y = average)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x="Number of Days in Month", y = "", subtitle = "Average Number of Articles Published", title = "Number of Articles Published Monthly Based on the Length of the Month")









The table below shows the most frequent lowercase words found in article headlines. Most of the words are very short in length, indicating that the New York Times prefers to keep words above 2-3 characters long capitalized. Notably, however, the words “special” and “report” both appear lowercased 34 times. Upon further inspection, I found that the New York Times ran an article series called “A special report”, reporting on important world-scale events. This series accounts for the otherwise strange appearance of these long lowercased words.


Code
lowercase <- NYTimes |> mutate(lowercase_words = str_extract_all(Title, "([^'-.\\&]\\b)[a-z][a-z|']*\\b")) |> unnest(lowercase_words) |> select(lowercase_words) |> mutate(lowercase_words = str_replace(lowercase_words, " ", "")) |> group_by(lowercase_words) |> summarize(count = n()) |> arrange(desc(count)) |> head(n=20) |> print()


# A tibble: 20 × 2
   lowercase_words count
   <chr>           <int>
 1 in                391
 2 to                346
 3 of                345
 4 the               319
 5 a                 287
 6 and               208
 7 for               195
 8 on                165

10 by                 55
11 as                 49

13 special            34
14 an                 32

The graph below shows the number of election-related articles published in each month in the period 1996-2006. The graph shows spikes in election-related articles in the months January, May, July, September, October, and November. This spike in articles from September through November matches my expectations for the data, since elections in the US occur in November, and September and October are heavy campaigning months. I was surprised to see the spikes in January and May, which I hypothesize are attributable to inaugurations and primaries, respectively. Although there are relatively few election related articles represented here, it is clear that their publication usually occurs around the time of significant political/electoral events.


Code
election_articles <- grouped_month |> mutate(election = str_detect(Title, "elect|vote|voting") | str_detect(Subject, "elect|vote|voting")) |> group_by(onlyMonth) |> filter(election == TRUE)# |> summarize(count = n())
ggplot(election_articles, aes(x=onlyMonth)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x="Month", y = "", title = "Number of Election-Related Articles by Month from 1996-2006", subtitle = "Number of Articles")

title: Emissions
text:
This dataset comes from Carbon Majors, who have compiled a database of emissions data dating back to 1854. The dataset provides insights on the direct operational emissions of 122 of the world’s largest oil, gas, coal, and cement producers, with data such as entity type, commodity, production level, and total emissions attributed to that entity. I accessed it via the TidyTuesday repo from May 21, 2024.
The dataset can be found here: https://carbonmajors.org/Downloads
The TidyTuesday repo can be found here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2024/2024-05-21
The following visualization shows the stark increase in the production of nearly every type of resource included in the dataset in recent years, except for thermal coal and natural gas. In addition, there is a clear major rise in oil, gas, coal, and cement production after around 1950, with production of most types increasing sharply until a little after 2000, at which point growth in production continues but at a lower rate.

title: Chess
text:
This dataset comes from Lichess.org via Mitchell J on Kaggle, representing over 20,000 games of chess collected from users on Lichess.org. Data includes players’ ratings, openings played, and outcome of the game (among other data). I accessed it via the TidyTuesday repo from October 1, 2024.
The dataset can be found here: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/datasnaek/chess/data
The TidyTuesday repo can be found here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2024/2024-10-01
The following visualization shows the relationship between the number of turns a chess game takes and the difference between the two players’ ratings. A positive rating difference indicates that the player playing white had a higher rating than their opponent, and a negative rating difference indicates that the player playing black had a higher rating for that game. The visualization suggests that when there is a large difference between players’ ratings, fewer games with over 100 turns are played when compared to games where players’ have a small difference in ratings.
